The archlute is a European plucked instrument that appeared around 1600, a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.321-5. Its construction is close to a Renaissance tenor lute with the extended neck of a theorbo, and it usually has 14 courses, the first six keeping a tuning of fourths enclosing a third. In the first half of the seventeenth century it was mostly used by plucked-string players for solo music; after the late seventeenth century, as bass lines became higher and faster, it became the main plucked continuo instrument, and it also appears in Corelli's trio sonatas and Handel's opera Giulio Cesare.
拱魯特琴為撥弦樂器，以琴頸延伸可奏出低音聲部中較高的音；因琴身與弦長不及西奧爾伯: The archlute is a plucked instrument whose extended neck lets it play the higher notes of a bass part; because its body and string length are smaller than the theorbo's, its tenor and bass registers are weaker in volume. Compared with the Baroque lute it usually has fourteen courses, the first six keeping the Renaissance lute tuning of perfect fourths enclosing a third, rather than forming a minor chord as the first six courses of the Baroque lute do. 拱魯特琴琴身主要採用楓木或雲杉製作共鳴箱，琴頸多用檀木或桃花心木以確保耐用性與音: The archlute's body uses maple or spruce for the soundbox, and the neck is mostly rosewood or mahogany, for durability and tone. The fingerboard is usually ebony or boxwood. The strings are traditionally gut, the bass courses being gut wound with metal wire, mostly copper or silver. The pegs are ivory or bone, for a noble appearance. The internal bracing is spruce, to strengthen the resonance of the sound wave and the instrument's tonal projection.
拱魯特琴的聆聽場合包括17世紀獨奏、三聲部奏鳴曲與歌劇通奏低音。柯雷利作品1與3: The archlute is heard in seventeenth-century solo music, in trio sonatas and in operatic continuo. Corelli's trio sonatas Op. 1 and Op. 3 have parts for first and second violin, bass instrument or archlute, and organ continuo, which shows that it could take the bass and harmony in chamber music. Handel's opera Giulio Cesare (1724) also specifies parts for archlute and theorbo. Zamboni's twelve sonatas of 1718 belong to the solo repertoire and are usually written in tablature.
拱魯特琴約於1600年發展為歐洲撥弦樂器，介於大型西奧伯琴與文藝復興次中音魯特琴: The archlute developed around 1600 as a European plucked instrument, standing between the large theorbo and the Renaissance tenor lute. For the first three quarters of the seventeenth century it was mostly a solo instrument and rarely used for figured bass; at the end of the century, as bass lines grew faster and higher and a cello or viola doubled the figured bass, it replaced the theorbo as the main plucked figured-bass instrument and also took over the melodic bass of the trio sonata, as in Corelli's Op. 1 and Op. 3. Handel's operas use it too: Giulio Cesare (1724) has an archlute and theorbo figured bass.

A beginner should first master the tuning of the first six courses, whose intervals are fourths enclosing a third; the whole instrument usually has fourteen courses. Solo music is mostly written in tablature, and the player must stop and pluck the strings as written. In continuo playing the player reads the figured bass and fills in chords above the bass line; because the body and string length are smaller, the tenor and bass are weaker, so clear stopping and steady plucking matter most.
